overview.what_it_is: Summarize Written Text is an integrated reading-and-writing task in which the test taker reads an academic passage, identifies its central message and essential supporting points, and synthesizes them into one accurate, formal, grammatically complete sentence.

format_facts.label: Source text
format_facts.value: A reading passage of up to 300 words.

format_facts.label: Main purpose
format_facts.value: Communicate the passage's main topic, central claim, and essential supporting ideas without adding personal opinion.

format_facts.label: Expected style
format_facts.value: Formal, objective, concise, and written mainly in the simple present tense.

format_facts.label: Final check
format_facts.value: Confirm sentence count, meaning, grammar, punctuation, spelling, vocabulary, and the permitted response length before submitting.

scoring_factors.name: Content
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the response accurately includes the central idea and the most important supporting points from the passage.

scoring_factors.name: Form
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the response follows the required one-sentence format and remains within the permitted response length.

scoring_factors.name: Grammar
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the sentence is structurally complete and uses clauses, verbs, agreement, punctuation, and linking devices accurately.

scoring_factors.name: Vocabulary
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the response uses precise, context-appropriate words and paraphrases the source without changing its meaning.

critical_rules: Write exactly one sentence, not two or more sentences joined only by full stops.
State the passage's central message before adding supporting information.
Include essential supporting points but normally omit examples, minor statistics, anecdotes, and repeated details.
Do not add personal opinions, outside knowledge, recommendations, or conclusions that are absent from the passage.
Paraphrase important ideas instead of copying long sections directly from the source.
Use linking structures that create one controlled sentence rather than a string of unrelated clauses.
Use the simple present tense when reporting what the passage explains, argues, suggests, or demonstrates.
Reserve time to proofread the complete sentence before submitting.

learning_goals: Explain the task format, timing, response requirements, and scoring factors.
Identify the passage's topic, writer's purpose, and central claim under timed conditions.
Separate essential supporting points from examples, repetition, and background detail.
Use topic sentences, repeated key concepts, and signal words to track the development of ideas.
Infer the meaning and importance of unfamiliar words without stopping to translate every term.
Paraphrase key information accurately while preserving the writer's original meaning.
Synthesize two or three important notes into one coherent sentence using controlled clause structures.
Proofread efficiently for grammar, punctuation, spelling, sentence count, and response length.

core_method.name: TOPIC–CLAIM–SUPPORT–SYNTHESIZE
core_method.summary: Read first for the subject and overall purpose, reduce the passage to one central claim and two or three essential supports, paraphrase those notes, combine them into one controlled sentence, and check the final response against the task rules.

steps.detail: Read the opening and closing parts quickly to identify the general subject, text type, and likely direction of the passage.
State the broad subject in a short noun phrase, such as online education, public figures and privacy, or traditional marriage customs.
Ask what the writer mainly says about the topic; express the answer as one complete proposition rather than a single keyword.
Choose two or three ideas that explain, justify, contrast with, or develop the central claim, while excluding examples and minor details.
Replace source wording with accurate alternatives, change word forms where useful, and keep technical terms when no safe substitute exists.
Build one main clause for the central message and attach supporting information with a relative clause, participle phrase, conjunction, or controlled subordinate clause.
Read the sentence from beginning to end and confirm that it is complete, accurate, concise, grammatical, punctuated correctly, and written as one sentence.

core_method.formula: The passage [reporting verb] that [central claim], while/because/although [support 1] and [support 2], indicating that [overall significance when explicitly supported].

techniques.name: Topic-before-detail reading
techniques.purpose: Prevent attractive examples or statistics from being mistaken for the main idea.
how_to: Read the title or opening sentence for the broad subject.
Ask what question the whole passage appears to answer.
Write the topic as a noun phrase of two to six words.
Reject any proposed topic that describes only one paragraph.
techniques.example: For a passage comparing online and traditional classrooms, write the topic as 'students' views of online education' rather than '43 percent of students.'
techniques.why_it_matters: A correct topic gives the summary a stable focus and makes it easier to judge which details are essential.
techniques.common_error: Choosing a memorable statistic as the topic because it is specific and easy to copy.

techniques.name: Topic-sentence and repetition scan
techniques.purpose: Locate the central claim and major paragraph points efficiently.
how_to: Underline the first sentence of each paragraph when it expresses a general idea.
Circle words or concepts repeated across several paragraphs.
Notice whether the final sentence confirms, qualifies, or predicts something about the topic.
Turn the repeated concepts into short notes rather than copying full sentences.
techniques.example: Repeated references to virtual education, traditional classrooms, student preference, and future growth suggest a claim about current preferences versus future expectations.
techniques.why_it_matters: Main ideas are usually developed across the passage, whereas examples often appear once and then disappear.
techniques.common_error: Assuming every first sentence is automatically a topic sentence without checking the rest of the paragraph.

techniques.name: Signal-word mapping
techniques.purpose: Distinguish claims, contrasts, causes, results, and examples.
how_to: Mark contrast signals such as however, although, despite, and whereas.
Mark cause-and-result signals such as because, therefore, consequently, and as a result.
Mark example signals such as for example, for instance, and such as.
Give priority to the ideas around contrast and conclusion signals, but usually omit the examples themselves.
techniques.example: In 'Online learning is popular; however, most students find traditional classrooms easier,' the contrast after 'however' is likely to be central.
techniques.why_it_matters: Signal words reveal the logical relationship between ideas and help reproduce that relationship accurately in the summary.
techniques.common_error: Listing ideas in source order without showing whether they contrast, support, or cause one another.

techniques.name: Essential-versus-example filter
techniques.purpose: Reduce the passage to information that must appear in the summary.
how_to: Label each note as claim, support, example, statistic, background, or repetition.
Keep the central claim and the strongest supports.
Convert several similar statistics into one general statement when exact figures are unnecessary.
Delete anecdotes, names, dates, and illustrations unless they are central to the writer's conclusion.
techniques.example: Replace several survey percentages with 'students generally prefer traditional classrooms despite expecting online education to expand.'
techniques.why_it_matters: A summary has limited space, so minor details can crowd out the information that earns content credit.
techniques.common_error: Including every number from the passage because numerical information appears objective.

techniques.name: Meaning-safe paraphrasing
techniques.purpose: Demonstrate vocabulary control without distorting the source.
how_to: Change the grammatical form, such as 'students prefer' to 'student preference for.'
Replace common words with context-appropriate equivalents, such as 'shows' with 'indicates.'
Combine related source phrases into a broader but accurate expression.
Retain specialised terminology when a synonym would be less precise.
techniques.example: Source idea: 'Media scrutiny should be supported.' Paraphrase: 'Public examination by the media is justified.'
techniques.why_it_matters: Successful paraphrasing reduces copying while preserving content accuracy and formal tone.
techniques.common_error: Replacing words individually with inaccurate synonyms that change the strength or direction of the claim.

techniques.name: Main-clause-first construction
techniques.purpose: Keep a long one-sentence response grammatically controlled.
how_to: Write a complete main clause containing the topic and central claim.
Check that the main clause could stand alone as a sentence.
Add only one supporting structure at a time.
Stop adding detail when the sentence becomes difficult to read or control.
techniques.example: Start with 'The passage argues that media scrutiny of public figures is justified' before adding the reasons.
techniques.why_it_matters: A strong main clause protects the response from fragments, run-on structures, and unclear sentence focus.
techniques.common_error: Beginning with several dependent clauses and losing control of the main subject and verb.

techniques.name: Relative-clause compression
techniques.purpose: Combine related notes about the same noun without producing another sentence.
how_to: Identify a repeated person, object, institution, or concept in two notes.
Write the first idea as the main clause.
Attach the second idea with who, which, or that.
Use commas for non-essential extra information and no commas when the clause identifies the noun.
techniques.example: A dowry, which originated as a parental gift and later developed several functions, remains part of marriage in some traditional cultures.
techniques.why_it_matters: Relative clauses allow compact synthesis while maintaining a clear relationship between ideas.
techniques.common_error: Using 'which' without a clear noun reference or creating a comma splice before the clause.

techniques.name: Unfamiliar-word inference
techniques.purpose: Continue reading efficiently when one or two words are unknown.
how_to: Identify whether the word functions as a noun, verb, adjective, or adverb.
Look for a familiar root, prefix, or suffix.
Use nearby definitions, contrasts, examples, or cause-and-effect relationships.
Decide whether the exact meaning is essential to the passage's main claim before spending more time on it.
techniques.example: If 'scrutiny' appears beside references to monitoring, investigation, and media attention, infer that it means close examination.
techniques.why_it_matters: The task tests comprehension of the whole passage, not translation of every individual word.
techniques.common_error: Spending several minutes trying to solve one low-importance word and losing writing time.

worked_examples.title: Choosing the stronger task summary
worked_examples.input: Summary A: 'The passage was about a test where people read and write.' Summary B: 'The Summarize Written Text item requires test takers to summarize a reading of up to 300 words in one sentence using correct form, grammar, and vocabulary.'
worked_examples.decoding: Both responses mention the general subject, but Summary A is vague and omits the defining requirements, whereas Summary B identifies the item type, the source length, the one-sentence rule, and important language expectations.
worked_examples.plan: Keep the specific task name, required action, source length, response form, and main language requirements; omit general or conversational wording.
worked_examples.model_answer: The Summarize Written Text item requires test takers to condense a passage of up to 300 words into one accurate sentence using appropriate form, grammar, and vocabulary.

annotations.part: The Summarize Written Text item
annotations.comment: Names the exact topic rather than referring vaguely to 'the passage.'

annotations.part: requires test takers to condense
annotations.comment: Uses a formal reporting structure and paraphrases the action 'summarize.'

annotations.part: a passage of up to 300 words
annotations.comment: Includes a defining task condition.

annotations.part: into one accurate sentence
annotations.comment: States the critical form requirement.

annotations.part: using appropriate form, grammar, and vocabulary
annotations.comment: Adds the main language-quality expectations without unnecessary examples.

worked_examples.title: Combining dowry notes with a relative clause
worked_examples.input: Notes: dowries began as gifts from parents; dowries developed several social and economic functions; dowries remain part of marriage in some traditional cultures.
worked_examples.decoding: All three notes concern the same noun, 'dowry,' so the historical origin and development can be compressed into a relative clause while the continuing cultural role becomes the main clause.
worked_examples.plan: Use 'a dowry' as the key noun, place origin and development inside a non-defining relative clause, and state its continuing use as the central present-tense claim.
worked_examples.model_answer: A dowry, which originated as a parental gift and later acquired several social and economic functions, remains part of marriage in some traditional cultures.

annotations.part: A dowry
annotations.comment: Introduces the main topic directly.

annotations.part: which originated as a parental gift
annotations.comment: Paraphrases the first note in a non-defining relative clause.

annotations.part: and later acquired several social and economic functions
annotations.comment: Adds the second historical point without starting a new sentence.

annotations.part: remains part of marriage
annotations.comment: Uses the main verb to express the most current and important claim.

annotations.part: in some traditional cultures
annotations.comment: Preserves the source's limitation and avoids an inaccurate universal claim.

worked_examples.title: Public figures and media scrutiny
worked_examples.input: Passage outline: Public figures receive intense media attention; politicians should be monitored because their decisions affect public policy; entertainers and other public figures earn money through public support; the writer argues that media scrutiny is therefore justified.
worked_examples.decoding: The central claim is that scrutiny is justified, while the passage gives two distinct reasons: political accountability and public dependence for income.
worked_examples.plan: State the argument first, join the two reasons with 'because,' and avoid adding a personal judgment about whether privacy is important.
worked_examples.model_answer: The passage argues that media scrutiny of public figures is justified because politicians must be monitored for decisions affecting public policy, while entertainers and other prominent individuals depend on public support for their income.

annotations.part: The passage argues that
annotations.comment: Uses an objective reporting phrase rather than presenting the view as the test taker's opinion.

annotations.part: media scrutiny of public figures is justified
annotations.comment: States the central claim clearly.

annotations.part: because politicians must be monitored
annotations.comment: Introduces the first supporting reason.

annotations.part: for decisions affecting public policy
annotations.comment: Explains why political monitoring matters.

annotations.part: while entertainers and other prominent individuals depend on public support for their income
annotations.comment: Adds the second reason and distinguishes it from the political argument.

worked_examples.title: Students' views of online education
worked_examples.input: Passage outline: Online learning is increasing; many students consider online colleges reliable; most still find traditional classrooms easier and often higher in quality; nevertheless, students expect education to become more virtual and technology-dependent.
worked_examples.decoding: The passage presents a contrast between students' current preference for traditional classrooms and their expectation that online education will continue expanding.
worked_examples.plan: Use the contrast as the organizing principle, generalize the survey details, and end with the future expectation.
worked_examples.model_answer: Although students increasingly regard online education as reliable, they generally find traditional classrooms easier and more effective, yet they expect learning to become more virtual and dependent on technology in the future.

annotations.part: Although students increasingly regard online education as reliable
annotations.comment: Concedes the positive view of online learning.

annotations.part: they generally find traditional classrooms easier and more effective
annotations.comment: Expresses the dominant current preference without listing every percentage.

annotations.part: yet
annotations.comment: Signals the second contrast between present preference and future expectation.

annotations.part: they expect learning to become more virtual
annotations.comment: Captures the passage's prediction.

annotations.part: and dependent on technology in the future
annotations.comment: Adds a related future development in a concise coordinated phrase.

items.when_to_use: Use when the text mainly provides factual information or describes a process.
Use when the passage presents a position supported by reasons.
Use when the conclusion is cautious, indirect, or based on evidence rather than stated as an absolute fact.
Use when findings, survey results, or research evidence form the basis of the central claim.
Use when the writer emphasizes an issue, contrast, benefit, risk, or relationship.
Use to introduce the principal reason supporting the central claim.
Use to add a simultaneous point or contrast two related groups or ideas.
Use to coordinate ideas of similar importance when the sentence remains easy to follow.
Use after a noun to add non-essential explanatory information in a relative clause.
Use to express a direct result of the preceding action without creating another full clause.
Use at the start of a dependent clause to acknowledge a contrasting fact before stating the main point.
Use before a noun phrase or gerund to show that one fact does not prevent another.
Use to contrast two categories, periods, approaches, or viewpoints.
Use cautiously within the sentence to mark a strong contrast, ensuring punctuation remains correct.
Use when the passage explicitly prefers, replaces, or distinguishes one alternative from another.
Use when the passage clearly describes a consequence of earlier information.
Use as a participle phrase to attach a result compactly.
Use when a previous process or condition produces a stated outcome.
Use when the writer draws a logical conclusion from previously stated evidence.
Use to introduce a conclusion directly supported by findings or evidence.
Use to convert 'X is growing' into a compact noun phrase.
Use to paraphrase statements saying that a group prefers one option.
Use to compress statements about necessity or obligation.
Use to paraphrase 'depends on' while connecting the idea to another noun phrase.

items.item: the effect of X on Y
items.when_to_use: Use to express a relationship between a cause, influence, or condition and its outcome.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: It violates the required response form even when the content is accurate.
common_mistakes.fix: Use one main clause and attach important supporting ideas with controlled subordinate or relative clauses.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing a vague statement such as 'The passage discusses education.'
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: It identifies only the topic and fails to communicate what the writer says about it.
common_mistakes.fix: Add the central claim and the most important relationship, contrast, cause, or conclusion.

common_mistakes.mistake: Including personal opinion or outside knowledge.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The response no longer represents the source objectively and may introduce unsupported information.
common_mistakes.fix: Use reporting language such as 'the passage argues' and include only ideas supported by the text.

common_mistakes.mistake: Copying long phrases or whole sentences from the passage.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: It limits evidence of vocabulary control and can produce an unfocused response containing unnecessary detail.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce each main idea to a short note, then rebuild it using different grammatical forms and accurate synonyms.

common_mistakes.mistake: Listing examples and statistics instead of summarizing the point they support.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Minor evidence consumes space while the central argument may remain unclear.
common_mistakes.fix: Generalize similar examples into one supporting statement unless an exact figure is essential to the conclusion.

common_mistakes.mistake: Joining many independent clauses with commas.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: This creates a comma splice or run-on sentence and weakens grammatical control.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a conjunction, semicolon where appropriate, or convert one idea into a dependent or relative clause.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using too many linkers in one sentence.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The logical structure becomes difficult to follow and the sentence may sound mechanical.
common_mistakes.fix: Choose one primary relationship, such as contrast or cause, and use only the linkers needed to express it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Changing the strength of the writer's claim.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Words such as 'may,' 'often,' 'some,' and 'generally' carry important limitations that affect meaning.
common_mistakes.fix: Preserve cautious language and quantity markers when paraphrasing.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The reader cannot identify which noun 'which,' 'who,' or 'that' refers to.
common_mistakes.fix: Place the relative clause immediately after its intended noun and reread the sentence for reference clarity.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: A correct summary can lose quality through subject-verb disagreement, missing punctuation, spelling errors, or an accidental second sentence.
common_mistakes.fix: Reserve the final one to two minutes for a fixed form-content-language check.

time_budget.focus: Review the one-sentence rule, timing, content expectations, scoring factors, and submission checklist.
Identify topics, topic sentences, repeated concepts, writer purpose, and central claims in short passages.
Separate essential supporting ideas from examples, statistics, background information, and repetition.
Transform source phrases through synonyms, word-form changes, noun phrases, and grammatical restructuring.
Combine notes using main clauses, relative clauses, contrast structures, and cause-and-result linkers.
Complete two timed summaries, then diagnose content, form, grammar, vocabulary, and editing problems.

drills.name: Six-word topic drill
drills.instructions: Read five short passages and express the topic of each in no more than six words before identifying the central claim.

drills.name: Claim or example sorting
drills.instructions: Label ten extracted statements as central claim, main support, example, statistic, background, or repetition, then explain which ideas belong in a summary.

drills.name: Signal-word reconstruction
drills.instructions: Remove the linkers from short paragraphs and choose suitable contrast, cause, result, or example signals to restore the original logic.

drills.name: Three-note compression
drills.instructions: Turn three short notes about one topic into a single sentence using one main clause and one dependent or relative clause.

drills.name: Paraphrase ladder
drills.instructions: Rewrite one source statement three times: first by changing word forms, second by using synonyms, and third by changing both vocabulary and sentence structure.

drills.name: Error-repair sprint
drills.instructions: Correct summaries containing a fragment, comma splice, unclear pronoun, inaccurate synonym, unnecessary example, or second sentence.

drills.name: Ten-minute simulation
drills.instructions: Spend approximately two minutes reading and marking, two minutes making notes, four minutes drafting, and two minutes checking one complete item.

practice_plan.routine: For every practice passage, follow the same sequence: identify the topic, write the central claim in plain words, choose two or three essential supports, cross out examples and repeated details, paraphrase the notes, construct one main clause, attach supporting information with no more than two controlled structures, and finish with a form-content-language check.

mastery_checklist: I can explain that the task requires one sentence written within 10 minutes.
I can identify the topic without confusing it with one example or statistic.
I can express the writer's central claim as a complete proposition.
I can select the strongest two or three supporting points.
I can omit minor examples, anecdotes, repetition, and unnecessary numerical detail.
I can preserve qualifications such as may, generally, some, and often.
I can paraphrase key ideas without changing their meaning.
I can create a complete main clause before adding dependent information.
I can use relative clauses, contrast clauses, and cause-and-result structures accurately.
I can keep the response formal, objective, and mainly in the simple present tense.
I can confirm that the response contains exactly one sentence.
I can proofread grammar, punctuation, spelling, vocabulary, and response length before submitting.
strategy_notes: The main idea is not always the first sentence; verify it against repeated concepts and the passage's conclusion.
A topic is a subject, while a central claim states what the writer says about that subject.
The best summary is not the longest response; it is the shortest response that preserves all essential meaning.
Examples help you understand the writer's point, but they usually do not need to appear in the final sentence.
When several statistics support the same conclusion, summarize the trend rather than copying each figure.
Use one clear grammatical backbone: subject, reporting verb, central claim, and selected support.
Do not force advanced vocabulary when a common academic word expresses the meaning more accurately.
A safe paraphrase preserves logical direction, quantity, certainty, comparison, and cause.
When the source contains contrast, the summary should normally preserve that contrast with although, while, whereas, despite, or yet.
When the sentence becomes difficult to read aloud in one pass, remove a minor detail or simplify one clause.
Punctuation is part of grammar control: commas should separate introductory clauses and non-defining relative clauses, not replace conjunctions between complete clauses.
Complete the response early enough to check whether an accidental full stop, abbreviation, or copied punctuation has created more than one sentence.

metadata.estimated_study_time: Plan to spend about 2 hours and 15 minutes on this chapter, including reading strategy work, summary-writing practice, grammar review, timed practice, and self-checking.
